questions.question: What is HashiCorp Vault and what problem does it solve?
options: A secrets management platform that centralizes storage, access control, and lifecycle management of secrets (tokens, passwords, certificates, encryption keys) — eliminates secrets sprawl and hardcoded credentials in applications
questions.explanation: Vault solves secrets sprawl: credentials scattered in config files, environment variables, wikis, and code repositories. Centralize all secrets in Vault with: audit logging, dynamic secrets, fine-grained access control, automatic rotation, and encryption as a service.

questions.question: What is Vault's secrets engine and name common types?
options: Components that store, generate, or encrypt data. Types: KV (key-value, static secrets), AWS/Azure/GCP (dynamic cloud credentials), Database (dynamic DB credentials), PKI (certificate authority), SSH (OTP/CA signing), Transit (encryption-as-a-service), LDAP, Kubernetes
questions.explanation: Secrets engines mounted at paths. KV v2: versioned key-value storage. AWS engine: generates IAM access keys with TTL (dynamic, auto-revoke). Database engine: generates DB credentials per request. PKI: issues X.509 certificates. Transit: encrypt/decrypt without storing data. Each engine at a mount path (e.g., secret/, aws/, database/).

questions.question: What is Vault authentication and name common auth methods?
options: Mechanisms for users and applications to prove their identity to Vault. Methods: Token (fundamental), AppRole (app-to-Vault), Kubernetes (K8s service accounts), AWS (IAM roles/EC2), LDAP/AD, GitHub, JWT/OIDC, TLS certificates
questions.explanation: Auth methods mounted at auth/ paths. Each method verifies identity differently. Result: a Vault token with attached policies. AppRole: role-id + secret-id (app credentials). K8s: pod's service account JWT → Vault token. AWS: IAM/EC2 identity → token. Token: fundamental building block — all auth returns a token.

questions.question: What is a Vault token and what are its properties?
options: The core identity mechanism in Vault — issued after authentication, attached to policies, has a TTL (time-to-live). Properties: policies (what it can access), TTL (expiry), max TTL, renewable, accessor (reference without revealing token), type (service/batch)
questions.explanation: Token properties: policies (list of policy names), TTL (expires in X seconds), max_ttl (cannot renew beyond), renewable (can be renewed before expiry), orphan (no parent), accessor (lookup without token). Service tokens: renewable, survive Vault restarts. Batch tokens: lightweight, not renewable, not stored.

questions.question: What is a Vault policy and how is it written?
options: HCL or JSON document that defines what paths a token can access and what capabilities are allowed — capabilities: create, read, update, delete, list, sudo, deny. Assigned to tokens at auth time
questions.explanation: Policy syntax: path 'secret/data/app/*' { capabilities = ['read', 'list'] }. Capabilities: create (write new), read, update (overwrite existing), delete, list (enumerate), sudo (root-restricted ops), deny (explicit deny overrides allow). Default policy: attached to all tokens (minimal permissions). Root policy: unlimited access.

questions.question: What is Vault's KV (Key-Value) secrets engine and difference between v1 and v2?
options: KV v1: simple key-value, no versioning, overwrite destroys old value. KV v2: versioned — keeps configurable number of previous versions, soft-delete (recover deleted versions), check-and-set (optimistic locking). Use v2 for production
v2 is encrypted by default only
questions.explanation: KV v2: vault kv put secret/app/config api_key=abc123. vault kv get secret/app/config. vault kv metadata get: see all versions. vault kv rollback -version=2: restore previous version. Deletion: soft-delete (vault kv delete) vs destroy (vault kv destroy — permanent). Max versions: configurable per secret or engine-wide.

questions.question: What is Vault's dynamic secrets and why are they preferred over static secrets?
options: Generated on-demand with a limited TTL — Vault creates real credentials (AWS IAM keys, DB passwords) when requested and revokes them automatically when TTL expires. No shared long-lived credentials; each app gets unique credentials
questions.explanation: Dynamic secrets advantages: short-lived (auto-revoked after TTL), unique per request (breach isolation), no rotation needed (automatically expire), audit trail per credential. AWS dynamic creds: Vault creates IAM user/role credentials, automatically deletes after lease expires. DB dynamic: creates DB user with TTL.

questions.question: What is a Vault lease and how does lease renewal work?
options: A time-limited grant of a secret or token — every dynamic secret and token has a lease with a TTL. Leases can be renewed (extend TTL) before expiry if they're renewable. Lease revocation: immediate secret invalidation
questions.explanation: Lease lifecycle: issue (with TTL) → use → renew before expiry (vault lease renew LEASE_ID) → expire (auto-revoke) OR revoke (vault lease revoke LEASE_ID). lease_duration: initial TTL. max_lease_ttl: hard ceiling, cannot renew beyond. Applications should renew leases proactively (Vault Agent automates this).

questions.question: What is AppRole authentication and when is it used?
options: Machine-to-Vault authentication using role-id (non-secret, can be hardcoded) and secret-id (secret, one-time use or limited use) — designed for automated pipelines and applications where a human can't log in interactively
questions.explanation: AppRole: role_id is like username (non-sensitive, embedded in app). secret_id is like password (sensitive, delivered separately). Secret IDs: single-use, n-use, or unlimited. TTL on secret IDs. Response wrapping: deliver secret-id securely wrapped. CI/CD: inject at deploy time. Principle: separate delivery of role-id and secret-id.

questions.question: What is Vault's Transit secrets engine?
options: Provides encryption-as-a-service — applications encrypt/decrypt data without storing it in Vault. Vault manages encryption keys; applications send plaintext, receive ciphertext. Key rotation: re-encrypt with new key version. Never stores the data itself
questions.explanation: Transit: vault write transit/encrypt/my-key plaintext=$(base64 <<< 'secret') → vault:v1:ciphertext. vault write transit/decrypt/my-key ciphertext=vault:v1:... → base64 decoded plaintext. Key rotation: vault write transit/keys/my-key/rotate. Rewrap: re-encrypt ciphertext with latest key version without decrypting. BYOK supported.

questions.question: What is Vault's PKI secrets engine?
options: Acts as an internal Certificate Authority — issues X.509 certificates on demand with configurable TTLs. Eliminates long-lived certificates by issuing short-lived certs (hours/days). Supports: Root CA, Intermediate CA, certificate signing, CRL distribution
questions.explanation: PKI engine: mount at pki/. Generate root CA (or import). Create roles (CN rules, SANs, TTL limits). Issue: vault write pki/issue/my-role common_name=app.example.com ttl=24h. Returns: certificate, private key, CA chain. ACME protocol support. Auto-rotation with short TTLs — better than long-lived certs.

questions.question: What is Vault's Database secrets engine?
options: Dynamically generates database credentials with configurable TTLs — connects to databases (MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Oracle, etc.) and creates time-limited user accounts on demand. Credentials auto-revoked when lease expires
questions.explanation: Database engine: configure connection (DB URL + admin credentials). Create role (CREATE USER SQL template, TTL). Request credentials: vault read database/creds/my-role → username + password. DB creates user. Lease expires → Vault drops user. Static roles: manage rotation of existing DB accounts on a schedule.

questions.question: What is Vault Agent and what problem does it solve?
options: A client-side daemon that handles Vault authentication and secret delivery to applications — auto-renews tokens and leases, caches secrets, writes secrets to files or environment variables. Applications don't need Vault SDK: agent handles auth
questions.explanation: Vault Agent: handles auto-auth (AppRole, K8s, AWS), auto-renews tokens/leases, template rendering (writes secrets to config files using ctmpl templates), caching (local proxy). Applications just read from file or connect to local Agent. Solves: application doesn't need to know Vault exists, restart recovery, TTL management.

questions.question: What is Vault's response wrapping?
options: A security mechanism that wraps a secret in a single-use token — the requester gets a wrapping token instead of the actual secret. Only the intended recipient who presents the wrapping token gets the real value. Detects interception (token used = someone intercepted)
questions.explanation: Response wrapping: vault kv get -wrap-ttl=60s secret/app/creds → wrapping_token. Deliver wrapping token (not secret). Recipient: vault unwrap WRAPPING_TOKEN → actual secret. If wrapping token already used: someone intercepted it (alert!). Use for: delivering AppRole secret-ids, initial credential delivery.

questions.question: What is Vault's audit device and why is it critical?
options: Logs every request and response in Vault in a tamper-evident log — critical for security compliance and forensics. Types: file (append to file), syslog, socket. Vault requires at least one audit device to be operational (blocks requests if all audit devices fail)
questions.explanation: Audit logs: contain timestamp, request type, path, token accessor, response (secrets redacted by HMAC). All access to secrets logged. File audit: append-only log file. Multiple audit devices: for redundancy. Vault BLOCKS all operations if all enabled audit devices fail to write — data integrity over availability.

questions.question: What is Vault's seal/unseal mechanism?
options: Vault starts sealed — encryption key (master key) is split using Shamir's Secret Sharing. Unsealing requires a quorum (e.g., 3 of 5 key shares) to reconstruct the master key. Sealed Vault cannot decrypt its storage. Auto-unseal: uses cloud KMS or HSM to unseal automatically
questions.explanation: Sealed Vault: data encrypted, inaccessible. Unseal: provide key shares (vault operator unseal) until threshold reached. Auto-unseal: AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, GCP Cloud KMS, HSM — Vault decrypts master key from KMS on startup automatically. Best practice: auto-unseal for HA. Manual unseal: for highest security air-gapped environments.

questions.question: What is Vault's High Availability (HA) mode?
options: Active-Standby cluster: one active node handles all requests, standby nodes ready to take over. Storage backend must support HA (Consul, Raft, DynamoDB, etcd). Vault Raft: built-in integrated storage without external dependency
questions.explanation: Vault HA: one active, N standbys. Standbys forward requests to active. Auto-failover: active dies → standby promoted. Raft consensus: built-in, no external Consul needed. Raft storage: automatic leader election. Load balancer: route to any node (standbys forward). Unsealing: each node must be unsealed separately.

questions.question: What is Vault Raft integrated storage?
options: Built-in distributed consensus storage for Vault — uses the Raft algorithm to replicate state across Vault cluster nodes. No external storage backend (Consul) needed. Data stored in /opt/vault/data directory on each node. Recommended for new deployments
questions.explanation: Raft: peer nodes defined in vault.hcl. Leader election: one leader handles writes. Followers: replicate state. Auto-pilot: automated cluster management (dead server cleanup, server stabilization). Snapshot: vault operator raft snapshot save to backup. Simpler than Consul backend — no external dependency.

questions.question: What is Vault's entity and alias system?
options: Vault identity: Entity (unique identity) composed of Aliases (auth method identities) — one entity can have aliases across multiple auth methods (LDAP user + GitHub user = same entity). Entities receive policies directly or via groups
questions.explanation: Entity: logical user/service. Aliases: token from LDAP auth + token from GitHub auth → same entity. Policies on entity apply regardless of which auth method used. Groups: internal (manually assign entities) or external (mapped to external AD groups). Entity metadata: custom key-value for access decisions.

questions.question: What is Vault's namespace feature (Enterprise)?
options: Vault Enterprise feature creating isolated multi-tenant Vault instances within a single Vault cluster — each namespace has its own auth methods, secrets engines, policies, tokens. Hierarchical namespaces for org structure. Enables Vault-as-a-Service
questions.explanation: Namespaces: tenant isolation without separate Vault clusters. Root namespace → child namespaces (e.g., team-a/, team-b/). Each namespace: completely isolated auth, policies, secrets. Tokens scoped to namespace. Admins delegate namespace management to teams. Enterprise feature — not in OSS.

questions.question: What is Vault's Kubernetes auth method?
options: Allows Kubernetes pods to authenticate with Vault using their ServiceAccount JWT tokens — pod sends SA token to Vault, Vault validates with Kubernetes API, issues Vault token. No secrets needed in pod spec; identity proven by K8s
questions.explanation: K8s auth: vault write auth/kubernetes/role/myapp bound_service_account_names=app-sa bound_service_account_namespaces=default policies=myapp-policy ttl=1h. Pod presents SA JWT (/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token). Vault validates with K8s TokenReview API. Returns Vault token with myapp-policy.

questions.question: What is Vault's path structure and naming convention?
options: Vault uses a hierarchical path structure: sys/ (Vault system), auth/ (auth method config), secret/ or ENGINE_NAME/ (secrets), cubbyhole/ (per-token private storage). Operations: read, write, list, delete on paths. Paths define what operations apply
questions.explanation: Path anatomy: METHOD/PATH. vault kv get secret/app/config = GET secret/data/app/config (KV v2 adds /data/). vault list auth/approle/role = list roles. sys/: Vault system info. cubbyhole/: private to current token, cannot be shared. mount paths: configurable, defaults like secret/, aws/, etc.

questions.question: What is the difference between Vault's service tokens and batch tokens?
options: Service tokens: stored in memory, renewable, can create child tokens, persist across restarts, heavier. Batch tokens: not stored (encoded in token itself), not renewable, no children, lighter weight, faster to create. Use batch for high-volume short-lived access
questions.explanation: Service tokens: default type. Renewable. Can have child tokens (orphan flag removes parent dependency). Persisted in storage. Good for: humans, long-running services. Batch tokens: encoded data, not stored. Not renewable. No children. Great for: short-lived Lambda functions, CI/CD jobs, high-throughput apps. TTL required.

questions.question: What is Vault's cubbyhole secrets engine?
options: A private key-value store scoped exclusively to the token that created it — other tokens cannot access it. Used for response wrapping (wrapped token stored in cubbyhole of wrapping token). Data deleted when token expires
questions.explanation: Cubbyhole: automatically mounted at cubbyhole/. Every token has its own cubbyhole, isolated from all others. No policy can grant access to another token's cubbyhole. Primary use: response wrapping (Vault stores wrapped value in cubbyhole of single-use wrapping token). Cannot be enabled/disabled — always present.

questions.question: What is Vault's secret ID accessor and token accessor?
options: A reference to a token or secret-id that allows operations (lookup, revoke) without exposing the actual token/secret-id value — accessible to administrators for auditing and revocation without knowing the actual credential
questions.explanation: Token accessor: opaque identifier stored in audit logs instead of actual token. Admin uses accessor to: look up token properties (vault token lookup -accessor ACC), revoke token (vault token revoke -accessor ACC). Cannot use accessor to make API calls. Secret-id accessor: similar for AppRole secret IDs.

questions.question: What is Vault's Secret Sync (1.13+)?
options: Syncs Vault secrets to external secret stores (AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager, GitHub Actions, Vercel) — applications that can't use Vault API directly can still get Vault-managed secrets via their native secret store
questions.explanation: Secret Sync: define sync destinations (AWS SM, Azure KV, etc.). Create sync associations: link Vault KV paths to destinations. Vault pushes secret updates to external stores. Applications use native SDK for their platform. Good for: legacy apps, platform-specific integrations, compliance requirements.

questions.question: What is Vault's OIDC auth method?
options: Authenticates users via OpenID Connect — integrates with identity providers (Auth0, Okta, Google Workspace, Azure AD) to enable SSO for Vault. Users log in with their corporate credentials via OIDC flow, receive Vault token with policies based on OIDC claims
questions.explanation: OIDC auth: configure provider URL, client ID, client secret. Define roles mapping OIDC claims to Vault policies. User: vault login -method=oidc role=engineer → browser opens → IDP login → callback → Vault token. Groups: OIDC groups → Vault policies (e.g., github.com org members → dev-policy).

questions.question: What is Vault's control group feature (Enterprise)?
options: Requires additional approvals before a secret can be accessed — define that sensitive paths require N approvers from a specific group. Requester gets a wrapping token; approvers authorize; requester unwraps to get the secret. Adds human approval step to secret access
questions.explanation: Control groups: path 'secret/data/pci/*' { capabilities = ['read'], control_group = { ttl = '1h', factor = { type = 'approvals', approvers = [group.infosec-team] }} }. Requester gets wrapping token. Approver: vault write sys/control-group/authorize REQUEST_ACCESSOR. Requester: vault unwrap TOKEN → secret. Full audit trail.

questions.question: What is Vault Performance Replication vs DR Replication (Enterprise)?
options: Performance Replication: primary cluster replicates token and lease state to secondary clusters for read scalability and geo-distribution — secondaries serve read requests locally. DR Replication: cold standby that replicates entire cluster state for disaster recovery, not for read scaling
questions.explanation: Performance: read scaling + reduced latency. Secondaries can service read requests. Primary still handles writes. DR: full state replica for disaster recovery. Primary fails → promote DR secondary. DR cluster not normally serving traffic. Enterprise feature. Both: cluster IDs, tokens valid across clusters with performance replication.

questions.question: What is Vault's token helper?
options: A command-line tool that stores the Vault token locally between CLI invocations — default: ~/.vault-token file. The vault CLI reads this file automatically. vault login: writes token. vault token revoke: removes. Custom token helpers can store tokens in OS keychain or credential managers
questions.explanation: Token helper: stores token between sessions. Default: ~/.vault-token plain text file — chmod 600 it. VAULT_TOKEN env var overrides file. vault login: authenticates and saves token. vault logout: revokes and removes. Custom: $HOME/.vault.d/token_helper.sh (returns token on 'get', stores on 'set'). Best practice: use VAULT_TOKEN in CI/CD rather than file.

questions.question: What is the Vault agent injector in Kubernetes?
options: Kubernetes MutatingWebhook that automatically injects Vault Agent sidecar containers into annotated pods — pod annotated with vault annotations gets a Vault Agent sidecar that authenticates with Vault, retrieves secrets, and writes them to shared memory volume for the main container
questions.explanation: Agent Injector: annotate pod with vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject: 'true', vault.hashicorp.com/role: 'myapp', vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-secret-db: 'database/creds/myapp'. Agent sidecar: auth → fetch secrets → write to /vault/secrets/. Init container renders secrets before app starts, sidecar renews. Zero code changes needed.

questions.question: What is Vault's TOTP secrets engine?
options: Generates and validates Time-based One-Time Passwords (TOTP/Google Authenticator) — stores TOTP keys in Vault and provides code generation/validation. Vault acts as the TOTP authenticator instead of a hardware device or phone app
questions.explanation: TOTP engine: store TOTP key in Vault. Generate current code: vault read totp/code/mykey → code. Validate code: vault write totp/code/mykey code=123456 → valid=true/false. Use cases: backup TOTP when user loses phone, centralized 2FA management, service account 2FA. Based on RFC 6238.

questions.question: What is a Vault root token and when should it be used?
options: A token with unlimited permissions that is created during vault operator init — should be revoked after initial setup and only regenerated when needed for emergency break-glass scenarios. Never use for day-to-day operations
questions.explanation: Root token: created during init. Use for: initial setup (create auth methods, enable engines, create policies). Immediately revoke after setup. Regenerate when needed: vault operator generate-root (requires unseal key quorum). Never store root token anywhere — only generate when absolutely necessary.

questions.question: What is Vault's performance standby nodes?
options: Enterprise feature: standby nodes that serve read requests (instead of forwarding to active) — increases read throughput. Locally cache active node's state. Write requests still forwarded to active. Allows horizontal scaling of Vault cluster for read-heavy workloads
questions.explanation: Performance standbys (Enterprise): standard standbys forward all requests to active. Performance standbys: serve reads locally from replicated state. Increased throughput for read-heavy workloads (KV reads, auth lookups). Writes still go to active leader. Configure: max_lease_ttl, ui, listener configs same as active.

questions.question: What does vault operator init do?
options: Initializes a new Vault cluster: generates the master encryption key, splits it into key shares (Shamir's Secret Sharing), and outputs the key shares + initial root token. Must be run once on a new Vault cluster before it can be used
questions.explanation: vault operator init -key-shares=5 -key-threshold=3: creates 5 key shares, 3 required to unseal. Outputs: 5 unseal keys + initial root token. Store securely (PGP encryption recommended: -pgp-keys). For auto-unseal: -key-shares=1 -key-threshold=1 (cloud KMS handles unsealing). Never lose unseal keys — no recovery without them.

questions.question: What is the Vault VSO (Vault Secrets Operator) for Kubernetes?
options: A Kubernetes operator that syncs Vault secrets to native Kubernetes Secrets — VaultStaticSecret and VaultDynamicSecret CRDs define what to sync. K8s apps use standard K8s Secrets without knowing about Vault. Operator handles auth, rotation, sync
questions.explanation: VSO: creates K8s Secret objects from Vault secrets. VaultStaticSecret: sync KV secret to K8s Secret. VaultDynamicSecret: sync DB/cloud dynamic credentials. VaultPKISecret: sync PKI certificates. Advantage: existing apps using K8s Secrets work unchanged. Auto-renew: operator refreshes credentials before expiry.

questions.question: What is Vault's SSH secrets engine?
options: Provides two SSH access modes: OTP (One-Time Password — Vault generates one-time SSH password for target host) and CA Signing (Vault signs SSH public keys as a CA — signed keys grant access without distributing authorized_keys). Eliminates persistent SSH keys
questions.explanation: SSH CA mode: user requests Vault to sign their SSH public key with TTL. Signed cert: valid for TTL, no need to add to authorized_keys on every host. Hosts trust Vault CA. OTP mode: Vault generates random password for specific host:user, host validates via vault-ssh-helper daemon. Both: audit trail, short-lived access.

questions.question: What is Vault's MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication)?
options: Vault Enterprise MFA: requires additional factor (TOTP, Okta, PingID, Duo) when accessing specific paths or logging in — step-up authentication for sensitive secrets or admin operations. Separate from OIDC provider MFA
questions.explanation: Vault MFA (Enterprise): define MFA methods. Create MFA enforcement: path 'secret/data/pci/*' requires TOTP. User reads secret → Vault prompts for MFA → user provides code → access granted. Or: login requires MFA before token issued. Duo/Okta/PingID: push notifications or codes.

questions.question: What is Vault's KMIP secrets engine?
options: Implements the Key Management Interoperability Protocol — allows KMIP-compatible applications (databases, storage arrays, backup software) to use Vault as their key management server without code changes. Vault manages crypto keys for legacy enterprise software
questions.explanation: KMIP: standard protocol for crypto key management. NetBackup, MongoDB FLE, MySQL TDE, VMware VSAN can all use KMIP to get encryption keys from Vault instead of their own key management. Enterprise feature. Mount at kmip/. Create scopes/roles, issue client certificates for KMIP client authentication.

questions.question: What is Vault's resource quotas?
options: Controls rate limiting and lease quotas per Vault path, namespace, or cluster — rate limit quotas: max requests/second. Lease count quotas: max number of active leases. Prevents abuse, ensures fair resource usage, protects cluster stability
questions.explanation: Rate limit quota: vault write sys/quotas/rate-limit/api-limit path='auth/approle/' rate=100 burst=150. Lease count quota: max leases per namespace. System quota: cluster-wide limits. Apply at: root level, namespace, or specific mount path. Returns 429 Too Many Requests when rate limited.

questions.question: What is the vault kv patch command?
options: Updates specific fields of an existing KV v2 secret without overwriting other fields — unlike vault kv put which replaces the entire secret. Useful for updating one key in a multi-key secret
questions.explanation: vault kv patch secret/app/config db_password=newpass123: updates only db_password, leaves other fields (api_key, environment, etc.) unchanged. Uses HTTP PATCH method. Requires KV v2. Without patch: must read-modify-write entire secret (risk of overwriting concurrent changes).

questions.question: What is Vault's dead letter queue for secret sync?
options: When secret sync to external stores fails, failed events are stored in a dead letter queue — allows administrators to investigate and replay failed sync operations rather than silently losing secret updates
questions.explanation: Dead letter queue: vault read sys/sync/destinations/TYPE/NAME/queue → list failed events. Purge: vault write sys/sync/destinations/TYPE/NAME/purge-queue. Events include: reason for failure, timestamp, secret path. Retry: re-trigger sync. Important for: ensuring external secret stores stay in sync with Vault.

questions.question: What is Vault's audit filter?
options: Allows filtering sensitive fields from audit logs — exclude specific headers, response fields from being logged. Use for compliance: avoid logging passwords even in HMAC form, exclude irrelevant high-volume paths from audit
questions.explanation: Audit log: by default logs all requests/responses with sensitive values HMAC-hashed. Audit filter (Enterprise): exclude certain paths from audit (high-volume health checks), exclude specific request/response fields. For compliance: ensure audit logs don't contain raw secrets (default already HMACs them).

questions.question: What is vault token create and what flags are important?
options: Creates a new token with specified properties: -policy (attach policies), -ttl (token lifetime), -use-limit (max uses), -orphan (no parent token), -display-name (human-friendly label), -period (renewable indefinitely if renewed within period)
questions.explanation: vault token create -policy=app-policy -ttl=1h -display-name=my-app. Orphan (-orphan): token doesn't expire when parent expires (useful for long-running services). Period (-period=1h): periodic token — stays valid as long as renewed within period (no max_ttl). -use-limit=1: single use token (for response wrapping).

questions.question: What is Vault's performance improvements with request forwarding?
options: Standby nodes in HA cluster forward write requests to active node transparently — clients can connect to any cluster node; standbys handle reads locally (performance standbys) or forward to active. Clients don't need to track which node is active
questions.explanation: Request forwarding: connect to standby → standby forwards to active (write) or handles locally (read, if performance standby). Client transparent: use load balancer pointing to all nodes. Vault header X-Vault-Request-Forwarded indicates forwarded request. Enterprise performance standbys: additional read throughput without external LB complexity.

questions.question: What is the purpose of vault operator generate-root?
options: Generates a new root token using a quorum of unseal keys — used for emergency access when no valid admin tokens exist. Requires same threshold of unseal keys as unsealing. Root token should be revoked immediately after completing emergency tasks
questions.explanation: Generate-root: vault operator generate-root -init (start). Each key holder: vault operator generate-root -nonce=NONCE (provide key share). After threshold reached: encrypted root token issued. Decrypt: vault operator generate-root -decode=TOKEN -otp=OTP. Use, then vault token revoke. Audit trail shows generation.

questions.question: What is Vault's AWS auth method?
options: Authenticates AWS EC2 instances and IAM principals with Vault — EC2: uses instance identity document signed by AWS. IAM: uses AWS credentials to sign a GetCallerIdentity request. Vault validates with AWS APIs. No passwords or secrets in application code
questions.explanation: AWS auth IAM method: application signs GetCallerIdentity request with IAM credentials → sends to Vault → Vault validates with AWS STS. Maps IAM role ARNs to Vault policies. EC2 method: PKCS7 signed instance document → Vault validates with AWS. Works for Lambda, ECS, EC2, CodeBuild — any IAM identity.

questions.question: What is vault lease renew vs vault lease revoke?
options: vault lease renew LEASE_ID: extends the TTL of a dynamic secret lease — can renew up to max_lease_ttl. vault lease revoke LEASE_ID: immediately invalidates a lease and its associated credentials (DB user deleted, AWS keys deleted). Use revoke for incident response
questions.explanation: Lease renewal: vault lease renew PREFIX/LEASE_ID -increment=3600 (extend by 1h). Cannot extend beyond max_lease_ttl. Applications should renew before expiry (Vault Agent automates). Revoke: vault lease revoke PREFIX/LEASE_ID -force (bypass errors). vault lease revoke -prefix PREFIX/: revoke all leases under a path.

questions.question: What is Vault's permission deny vs absence of permission?
options: Explicit deny: a policy contains deny capability → always blocked regardless of other policies. Absence: no policy grants access → also denied (default deny). Deny beats allow: even if another policy allows, deny in any policy wins. Important for restricting subsets
questions.explanation: Policy evaluation: all attached policies evaluated. Any allow in any policy grants access. But deny in any policy overrides all allows. Use deny carefully — can lock out users unexpectedly. path '*' { capabilities = ['deny'] } blocks everything. Usually absence-of-permission is sufficient for access control.

questions.question: What is the Vault agent auto-auth and how does it work?
options: Automatically authenticates Vault Agent with Vault and maintains a valid token without manual intervention — Agent logs in, gets token, renews before expiry, re-authenticates if token expires. Supports: AppRole, AWS, K8s, Azure, GCP, JWT/OIDC auth methods
questions.explanation: auto_auth block in vault agent config: method 'kubernetes' { mount_path = 'auth/kubernetes', config = { role = 'myapp' } }. Agent reads K8s SA token, authenticates, gets Vault token, writes to sink file. sink type='file' { path='/home/vault/.vault-token' }. Renews automatically. App reads token from sink.
